distillation_scope: First-layer pure disease leaf for Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia. Central-line infection, neutropenia, pneumonia, UTI, ecthyma gangrenosum, endocarditis, resistant phenotype, and other foci are represented as source, host, complication, or treatment-context axes rather than disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Portal or source entry into blood
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: P. aeruginosa enters blood from a pulmonary, catheter/device, urinary, wound, burn, mucosal, abdominal, or initially occult source. The source shapes presentation and source-control needs but is not part of the first-layer disease name.

Density and persistence of viable organisms in blood; drives positive blood cultures, recurrent bacteremia, systemic inflammation, metastatic seeding, and treatment failure when coverage or source control is inadequate.

TLR4, complement, neutrophil, monocyte, IL-6/TNF/IL-1, and acute-phase activation from invasive gram-negative bacteremia; produces fever or blunted fever, rigors, tachycardia, leukocyte changes, CRP/PCT rise, and constitutional illness.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pseudomonal septic shock and organ dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endotoxin, cytokine, endothelial leak, vasoplegia, hypoperfusion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and microvascular injury causing hypotension, lactate rise, AKI, ARDS, DIC, encephalopathy, and death risk.

Pseudomonal elastases, phospholipases, pyocyanin, type III secretion effectors, vascular invasion, thrombosis, and necrosis can produce ecthyma gangrenosum, necrotizing skin or mucosal lesions, and necrotizing cavitary pneumonia.

Neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, transplant or steroid immunosuppression, burns, renal failure, advanced age, diabetes, structural lung disease, and severe comorbidity impair containment and increase invasive, recurrent, or necrotizing disease.

P. aeruginosa biofilm on central lines, dialysis catheters, urinary catheters, cardiac devices, prosthetic material, wounds, or endovascular surfaces can sustain relapse despite apparently active antibiotics.

Inactive empiric therapy, inducible AmpC, efflux, porin loss such as OprD, ESBL or metallo-beta-lactamase acquisition, underdosing, renal replacement dosing errors, or emergent resistance prolong bloodstream burden.

Persistent bloodstream infection can seed valve/device surfaces, septic thrombus, liver or soft tissue abscesses, bone, joints, eye, CNS, or other deep foci, increasing duration, source-control needs, and mortality.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia co-move through cytokine and sympathetic tone.
Elevated lactate marks higher shock severity.
WBC and ANC usually co-move except lymphocyte-predominant or marrow-suppressed states.
Both rise with invasive bacterial inflammatory burden, though kinetics differ.
Active therapy shortens bacteremia persistence if source control is adequate.
Device removal or drainage reduces persistent seeding.
Longer bacteremia raises deep seeding hazard.
Persistent bacteremia raises valve/device biofilm hazard.
Ecthyma gangrenosum in bacteremia often marks invasive vascular disease and severe host vulnerability.
MDR probability reduces chance that a standard empiric regimen is active.
Shock is the dominant early mortality pathway.
AKI indicates organ dysfunction and complicates antibiotic exposure.
ARDS and respiratory failure increase mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefepime effect requires susceptibility and adequate exposure.
MDR or evolving AmpC/efflux resistance can cause clinical failure.
Renal failure changes exposure and neurotoxicity risk.
Undrained or retained source prevents clearance.

side_effects.interpretation: Cefepime neurotoxicity risk rises with renal failure or high exposure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Active beta-lactam option when susceptibility and dosing context support it.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad antipseudomonal beta-lactam option when susceptibility and severity context allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Meropenem requires susceptibility and adequate exposure.
Carbapenem resistance or OprD loss makes meropenem unreliable.
Renal replacement therapy changes dosing.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad antipseudomonal carbapenem option when resistance risk and susceptibility context support it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Activity depends on susceptibility.
Often considered when standard beta-lactams are unreliable, but susceptibility is still required.

supportive_care: Obtain blood cultures and clinically indicated source cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay therapy in shock.

Assess pre-culture Pseudomonas context: neutropenia, high-dose steroids, transplant, structural lung disease, burn/wound, water exposure, prior broad antibiotics, recent hospitalization, and indwelling devices.
Use early sepsis resuscitation for shock: fluids, vasopressors, oxygen or ventilatory support, lactate reassessment, renal support, and ICU-level monitoring when unstable.

Reassess source control repeatedly: remove or exchange infected lines/devices when indicated, drain abscesses, debride necrotic tissue, and evaluate valve/device/endovascular foci when bacteremia persists or recurs.
Treat culture species, susceptibility, and resistance mechanism as confirmatory or post-workup treatment context; presentation-only diagnosis should not hard-code organism identity.
Adjust antipseudomonal antibiotic exposure for renal failure, dialysis, CRRT, critical illness pharmacokinetics, allergy, and local resistance ecology.
Repeat blood cultures and broaden source search when fever, shock, or bacteremia persists despite apparently active therapy.

Avoid collapsing this leaf into pneumonia, neutropenia, central-line infection, UTI, ecthyma gangrenosum, endocarditis, or resistant phenotype; those are source/context/risk/treatment modifiers or future leaves.
quality_notes: No treatment-rank labels are encoded; treatment ranking should emerge from forward simulation and context axes.
Pseudomonas species identity and susceptibility are not required ranking evidence in presentation-only cases.
